name: Aaron Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Kessler Appliances, on the press line that stamps the steel for washing machines, the side panels, the tops, the drum parts. A press is basically a giant hammer with a shaped die in it, that's the mould, and it comes down with a few hundred tonnes and the flat sheet comes out a panel. I'm the line lead on early shift, six presses in a row with transfer arms between them. I spend my day listening, watching for splits in the steel, and deciding when to stop the line before it costs us money.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's your life outside work like right now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Mila, she's a receptionist at a dental clinic, and we're saving for a deposit on a flat. We've got around four months of money put by, most of which is meant for that. I play five-a-side football on Thursdays with Tomasz, he sets the dies on our line. I use AI now and then, mostly to translate the German press manuals, because half of them never got translated properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So, more or less how things are now. Fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, one less thing to worry about. People have been saying robots are coming for twenty years. At Kessler we've had robot arms between the presses since before I started, and I'm still here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved, but not that surprised. The translation thing is handy and that's about as far as I've used it. If it stays a handy tool, my job stays my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, keep saving for the flat. We'd probably buy something next year, a two-bed out near the tram line, if the prices behave. I wouldn't change anything at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a Sunday where nothing's planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the flat you have in mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a new block going up near the last tram stop, the cheaper end of town. Two bedrooms, a little balcony. Mila wants it for the balcony, I want it for the parking. We'd need about another six months of saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI more if it stayed like this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a bit. Tomasz uses it to check his die settings against the spec sheet. If it actually saved me time, sure. I'm not against it, I just don't go looking.

S0.say: He'd say it's one less thing to worry about and point out that robot arms have been on his press line for years without taking his job.
S0.think: He'd be relieved but not surprised, seeing AI as a handy translation tool and no more. If it stays that way, his job stays his.
S0.do: Keeps going as normal and keeps saving for a flat deposit. Plans to buy a two-bedroom flat near the tram line next year if prices behave.
S0.feel: Calm, like a Sunday with nothing planned.
S0.quote: Mila wants it for the balcony, I want it for the parking.
S0.fieldNote: Aaron is practical and settled, with life plans centred on buying a flat with his girlfriend. He uses AI only when it clearly helps. He notes robots on his line have not replaced him so far, which shapes his calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. That sounds like what most people at work expect, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's like any other change, you adapt or you get left behind. Some jobs go, others come. I'd say that at the canteen and mean it, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd guess the press line gets more automatic and they need fewer people per shift, maybe four instead of seven. As lead I'd probably stay. But that means I'd be the one standing there when they tell the others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the AI tools properly, for fault logs and planning, once I saw Tomasz and the maintenance guys getting value from them. I'd keep saving but hold off on the flat for six months to see how things settle at Kessler. If the company offered courses on the new systems, I'd sign up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not losing sleep, but I'd be checking the noticeboard more often.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it be like being the one who stays?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Awkward. I'd have to train the new system while some of the people who taught me are being moved off. One of them, Henk, showed me how to read a split before it happens. I'd feel like I owed him something I couldn't pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why hold off on the flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a mortgage is thirty years and I'd want to know where I'd be in two. Mila would be annoyed, she's been looking at balconies for a year. Six months, I'd tell her. Just six.

S1.say: He'd say it's like any other change: you adapt or get left behind, with some jobs going and others arriving. He'd say it in the canteen and mostly mean it.
S1.think: He expects fewer people per shift and thinks he'd stay as lead, but would have to watch others being moved off. He feels he'd owe colleagues who trained him.
S1.do: Starts using AI tools properly for fault logs and planning once colleagues show it works. Keeps saving but holds off on the flat for six months, and would sign up for company courses on new systems.
S1.feel: Uneasy, checking the noticeboard more often but not losing sleep.
S1.quote: I'd feel like I owed him something I couldn't pay.
S1.fieldNote: Aaron would adapt once he saw others succeed, which fits his steady nature. His discomfort is about surviving while mentors are moved off. The flat purchase becomes his gauge of how secure he feels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay, that's a different conversation altogether.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is something the government and the companies need to get ahead of, and quickly. No point blaming the technology. Somebody has to work out how people pay rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think my job is probably gone within a year of it arriving. The transfer arms are already robots. Give the presses something that can hear a split coming and change the die itself, and they don't need a lead. My four months suddenly isn't a deposit, it's a life jacket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The flat would be off, straight away. That money becomes our emergency fund. I'd cut back on everything, no holiday, cheaper phone plan. I'd talk to Mila about whether we can live on one wage for a while, and I'd look around fast for anything near Kessler that still needs people on the floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd wake up at four, which is my alarm time anyway, but I'd be wide awake long before it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mila about the flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not no, it's not now. She'd cry a bit, probably, then she'd get practical, she's more practical than me. She'd have a spreadsheet by the weekend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomasz. He's the best die setter I know, but he's got a baby on the way. He'd need a job more than I would. We'd probably end up applying for the same things, which would be strange.

S2.say: He'd say government and companies must get ahead of this quickly and that blaming the technology is pointless. Someone must work out how people pay rent.
S2.think: He thinks his job would likely go within a year of AGI arriving, since the line is already partly robotic. His flat savings would turn into a life jacket.
S2.do: Calls off the flat immediately and turns the deposit into an emergency fund. Cuts back on holidays and phone costs, discusses living on one wage with his girlfriend and looks quickly for floor jobs nearby.
S2.feel: Alarmed, waking well before his four o'clock alarm.
S2.quote: My four months suddenly isn't a deposit, it's a life jacket.
S2.fieldNote: The fast scenario forces Aaron to drop his flat plans immediately. He blames no one and looks for practical fixes. He worries for a friend with a baby on the way and anticipates competing with him for jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I'd be thirty-two. That's long enough to do something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for people to retrain if someone helps them do it. I'd say companies like Kessler should be offering that now, not in year four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think five years is enough for me to get a second skill. I'd want something they'd still need people for longest, maybe the electrical side of maintenance, wiring and fixing the robots. After 2031, I genuinely don't know, but it's better than nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start a part-time maintenance electrician course at the technical college, two evenings a week, once I saw a couple of others from work doing it. We'd keep saving and probably push the flat back two years. I'd keep doing my job well, because a good reference matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But a working kind of anxious, if that makes sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait until you saw others doing it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm not a first-in kind of guy. I want to know the course is any good, that people get jobs from it. If Tomasz did it and said it was worth the money, I'd sign up the next week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do once it arrived in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hope the maintenance side holds out a few more years. Maybe move to wherever they're building the robots, not running them. I'd have to see. I wouldn't pretend I'd have a plan for that bit.

S3.say: He'd say five years is enough for people to retrain if someone helps them, and that firms like his should offer training now.
S3.think: He believes five years is enough to gain a second skill, ideally maintenance electrics. He admits he doesn't know what happens after 2031.
S3.do: Starts a part-time maintenance electrician course two evenings a week once colleagues vouch for it. Keeps saving and pushes the flat back two years while keeping up good work for a strong reference.
S3.quote: If Tomasz did it and said it was worth the money, I'd sign up the next week.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Aaron plans retraining but waits for proof from people he trusts. He is honest that his plan only buys time. The flat remains the thing he adjusts first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's practically a whole career away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if we start now and don't waste it. Retrain, plan, don't panic. I'd tell the young guys on the line to learn something on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel okay about it. I'd probably still buy the flat, because ten years of rent is a lot of money gone. I'd just do the electrician course over a few years and keep my options open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the flat in the next year, a cheaper one so the mortgage stays small. I'd start the electrician course in year two or three, after seeing how it worked for others. I'd keep going at Kessler as long as they needed me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Mostly okay, but the end point's still the end point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd still take on a mortgage knowing this was coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. If I'm paying someone's mortgage anyway through rent, I'd rather it was mine. A smaller one, though, so if things go wrong we could cover it from Mila's wage. That's the compromise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the 'end point' that still bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being thirty-seven, with a mortgage, when nobody needs a press lead or an electrician anymore. I can plan for ten years. I can't plan for what's after it.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is plenty if people start now, retrain and plan without panicking. He'd urge young colleagues to learn something on the side.
S4.think: He'd feel mostly okay and would still buy the flat, seeing rent as money lost. He'd do the electrician course gradually and keep options open.
S4.do: Buys a cheaper flat within a year so the mortgage stays small enough for one wage. Starts the electrician course in year two or three after seeing it work for others, and keeps going at his plant as long as he is needed.
S4.feel: Uneasy: mostly fine, but bothered by the eventual end point.
S4.quote: I can plan for ten years. I can't plan for what's after it.
S4.fieldNote: The long timeline lets Aaron keep his life plans, with the mortgage sized as a hedge. His retraining starts late and only after proof from others. He is calm about the decade itself but uneasy about the destination.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. The flat goes, the job goes, all in the same year, and there's nothing you can do in that time. What would help is honest notice from the company, a course I could do around my shifts, and some kind of support so we could keep paying rent while I switched.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what we're doing now. Because honestly, the answer is nothing much. Everyone at work talks about it on break, then we go back and run the presses. Me included.

headlineQuote: Everyone at work talks about it on break, then we go back and run the presses. Me included.
portrait: Aaron Bauer is twenty-seven, the early-shift lead on a steel press line at an appliance factory, living with his girlfriend Mila, a dental receptionist, and saving four months' money for a flat deposit. He uses AI now and then, mainly to translate press manuals, and adopts new things once trusted colleagues show they work. He is calm if AI fizzles and uneasy with steady change, using the flat as his gauge of security. AGI in two years leaves him alarmed and cancelling the flat, while five years pushes him into an electrician course once a friend vouches for it. With ten years he would still buy a smaller flat and retrain slowly, uneasy only about what comes after.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because the flat and the job would go in the same year with no time to act.
whatWouldHelp: Honest notice from the company, a course he could fit around shifts, and support to keep paying rent while he switched.
